Question: What is the biological/biochemical role of oxalic acid in plants?
Answer: Interesting question; it made me look it up. Oxalate in plants plays roles in photosynthesis, detoxification of environmental metals, and regulation of calcium metabolism. Needle-like oxalate crystals in plant tissues make them disagreeable or even harmful to browsing and grazing animals ranging from snails and slugs to cattle and deer, thus protecting plants from overconsumption. In agriculture, oxalate improves harvest quality.[1][2][3] Calcium is a vital mineral for all living organisms, yet too much of it can be toxic for reasons related to cell phosphates. All living organisms need phosphate for such functions as DNA, RNA, and ATP synthesis; regulating exocytosis (secretion of hormones, neurotransmitters, and other substances); pH buffering; muscle contraction; the structure of animal bones and shells; and the beating of cilia and flagella. But phosphate reacts with calcium to produce calcium phosphate crystals, fatal to cells. Thus, cells need to carefully regulate cytoplasmic calcium levels, and oxalate plays an important role in that. Some plant foods we consume are much higher in oxalate than others. Here’s an sidebar from one of my textbooks on why not to eat oxalate-rich vegetables if you need a fractured bone to heal.

Question: Why is human copulation length so long in comparison to other mammals?
Answer: Human infants are born in a very helpless state compared to the infants of other apes and monkeys. They require long-term parental care (months) before they can even walk and feed themselves, and much longer (years) before they can function in our complex human societies and be able to take care of themselves without parental involvement. To raise successful, surviving offspring has depended, through most of human existence, on cooperation between both parents. Especially in the absence of the modern conveniences of recent centuries, solitary parents probably had significantly lower rates of reproductive success, as do those of many other animal species. To help ensure biparental care and reproductive success, stong emotional bonding between mates is highly important. And there is no greater way of creating that emotional bond than sex. Most human sex acts, by far, are for pleasure, not for producing offspring. Outside of the basic necessities of erection and ejaculation, even the neurological wiring of our brains and genitalia serves more for pleasure than for procreation; aside from erection and ejaculation, it’s been hard or fruitless to find evidence of orgasm in more than a very few nonhuman species. This explains the high frequency of human copulation, and why human copulation is independent of periods of fertility. As for the duration of an individual act of copulation, that isn’t very long and is exceeded by some other animal species. One study of 500 couples around the world found that copulations lasted from 33 seconds to 44 minutes, averaging 5.4 minutes.[1] That’s really not all that long. Domestic dogs stay locked in copulation for 5 to 10 minutes, and some worms copulate nonstop for 20 years or more. A survey of sex therapists reported, on the basis of their counseling experiences with clients, that most found 7 to 13 minutes to be optimal and desirable, with durations outside this range being too short or too long.[2] Even 5 minutes, though, is much longer than necessary to achieve fertilization. Perhaps we copulate longer than necessary for the same reason we chew food or hold a sip of wine longer in the mouth than necessary tp swallow it—for pleasure, and because pleasure positively affects reproductive success. The article I cite above [1] also describes another hypothesis. We know that the penises of other animals (such as damselflies in one famous study) are anatomically shaped to compete with other males by scooping out the sperm of any male that has previously, but recently, mated with that female. This is a large area of animal behavior theory called sperm competition. Maybe the 5+ minute copulations of humans evolved to serve that purpose as well, with the ridge at the base of the penile head (glans) being the scooper. Damselfly penises—designed for sperm competition by scooping out the sperm of competing males. Variety of penises in nonhuman primates.

It’s very similar to the way hair grows, even though all the hair you can see is dead cells. In fact, almost everything you see when you look at another person is dead! Occasionally, in females with mild signs and symptoms of Turner syndrome, the diagnosis is delayed until the teen or young adult years. Girls and women with Turner syndrome need ongoing medical care from a variety of specialists. Regular checkups and appropriate care can help most girls and women lead healthy, independent lives.

Question: Is the theory of evolution a theory that cannot be proven or disproved?
Answer: In science, we do not say a theory is ever proven. We say it is the best explanation we have, consistent with a large body of compelling evidence. We must always be open to the possibility of modification or even falsification if new evidence demands it. But on the other hand, a theory can be disproven if there is evidence showing it cannot possibly be right. That said, there really is no such thing as “the theory of evolution.” Evolution is a natural, verified, observable process, like gravity or rain. Theories are our best evidence-based explanatoins of how evolution works. Natural selection is the predominant theory explaining most evolution, but different aspects of evolution call for different theories—sexual selection, for one. In principle, any of the theories of evolution could be disproved if there was evidence enough to falsify it. For example, Lamarck’s theory of evolution by inheritance of acquired characteristics was once popular, but it’s easily disproven by a great deal of evidence and therefore it was long ago discarded. (There is a slight lamarckian flavor in epigenetics—transgenerational but nonmutational phenotypic change—but not enough to matter to this argument.) There is no evidence, however, falsifying natural selection or sexual selection, but a world of evidence demonstrating their truth.

Question: What would theoretically happen if our mitochondria kept increasing? What would be the pros and cons?
Answer: Ah, the paradox of mitochondria. We die sooner because of them, yet we’d die instantly without them! A point to bear in mind is that one cause of mutations and of the degradation of proteins and other organic molecules is oxidative damage—akin to the rusting of iron and the way rubber bands become inflexible and useless with age. The chief cause of oxidative damage in the body is highly reactive molecules called free radicals. The biggest producer of free radicals is one’s own mitochondria. Mitochondria were classically recognized as the organelles that produce the energy required to drive the endergonic processes of cell life, but now they are considered as the most important cellular source of free radicals, as the main target for free radical regulatory and toxic actions, and as the source of signaling molecules that command cell cycle, proliferation and apoptosis.[1] Mitochondria thus contribute greatly to oxidative stress on the body, and this is one of the major causes of aging and the limitation on human life span.[2] Therefore, an excess of mitochondria might just cause more molecular damage to our DNA, proteins, etc.; faster molecular deterioration of the body; and shorter life spans. It would also require you to eat more, because mitochondria are the main consumers of the calories you take in. So your grocery bill could go up—but at least you wouldn’t live as long, having to pay this increased cost as long, so maybe that’s some consolation. Another byproduct of mitochondria, besides free radicals, is heat—lots of it. Most of your body heat comes from mitochondria. So if you had a superabundance of mitochondria, you’d also need new or increased means of getting rid of body heat, or else you’d face death from hyperthermia. Most likely, you’d sweat a lot more and your laundry bill might go up along with your food bill. An alternative and supplemental way of getting rid of body heat, however, is to have more blood vessels close to the skin surface so heat can radiate from the body more effectively. Even the ones we already have dilate to do this, which is why we may look red and flushed in the face when hot. If some race of future humans had this adaptation to go along with the greater abundance of mitochondria, they might be cherry-red people who sweat a lot. All in all though, it’s probably better not to have more mitochondria than necessary to meet a cell’s energy needs. Mitochondria come at a cost. While they’re indispensible to your life, they’re also killing you at the same time.

Question: Why did we evolve to have so many nerve endings in our anuses?
Answer: That’s so we can tell when the ghost peppers have left our system, or when yesterday’s chili was hot enough. Otherwise we might be oblivious to this vital information. To be a more serious, though, every body orifice is a potential route of invasion by other organisms. If we think of prehistory and our distant, naked ancestors sitting and sleeping on the ground—or even the various tribes of bush people today—it’s not far-fetched to conceive of other organisms attempting to invade the body by way of nose, ears, mouth, anus, urethra, or vagina. Not only do we have dense sensory nerve endings at these openings, but also high concentrations of immune cells (lymphocytes) and protective secretions (mucus, earwax) on guard against invasion, especially by microbes. One possible anal invader for our ancestors might have been blow flies and other fly species, attracted by the fecal odor there. The adult flies wouldn’t stay to occupy the anal canal or rectum, but would lay their eggs there. Their larvae (maggots) could then live there feeding on the abundance of bacteria to be found, or even chewing away at anorectal tissues as some maggots do. Sheep are very prone to perianal maggot infestations if nothing is done to prevent it; it’s a disease called sheep strike, and can destroy an entire flock. This is why ranchers bob the tails of lambs at birth, so a long natural tail doesn’t get contaminated with urine and feces and attract flies to the anus. For a prehistoric cave person or modern bush person, it would pay to feel a tickle or itch if a fly was crawling or laying eggs there, and (even in his/her semi-sleep) scratch it away. In some primitive cultures today, the floors of their huts are crawling with parasitic and scavenging arthropods—bedbugs, fleas, lice, and more. That’s a reason for sleeping on elevated platforms that make it a little harder for those organisms to invade the body. (The chigoe flea is a good example, if you want to read up on that). A bit of anal scratching when irritated would help further to repel such invaders (yet it also helps the spread of pinworms).

Question: How close are we to being able to extend a healthy human lifespan to 150 years and beyond?
Answer: First I want to make a difference between life span and life expectancy. Life span means the longest that any human being (or other species) has been known to live (with sound documentation—you can spare me your bible quotes). It is one fixed number and will always be the world record holder at any given time. The current human life span is a little over 122 years; the record holder is a French woman, Jeanne Calment (1875–1997). Life expectancy means the age at which the average person (or other species) in a population dies or, for persons of a given age group, how much longer they can expect to live on average. In a previous discussion, I’ve discussed these and provided a table of world life expectancies by country.[1] In the United States, life expectancy has been declining lately—that is, people are dying younger on average. I expect what you mean by the question is whether we’re approaching a time when the average person can live to 150—not just an extreme record holder. I don’t believe we’re anywhere near that (we’re barely approaching 80 now in the US), and because of the multiple unavoidable factors that cause tissue and organ degeneration, I doubt that we’ll ever average 150. I also think it would be disastrous to society if we were to do so, and make life miserable for everyone. Countries from the US to China are already facing problems with their populations getting too old. Greatly extending life expectancy is undesirable on multiple levels. If we got to a life expectancy of 150 or 200 years, governments and private citizens would regret it and probably curse the science that made it so. Question: What is the estimated number of people with an extra X chromosome?
Answer: This is a Quora Prompt Generator question, not being asked by a person, and it’s flawed. But it’s something that interests me, and considering other human-to-human questions recently, some actual human beings in Quoraland may be interested in the information. So here goes. Either a male or a female can have an extra X chromosome. In males, such individuals have two X’s and one Y, or in other words, XXY instead of the normal XY male condition. This is called Klinefelter syndrome and reportedly occurs in about 1 out of every 500–1000 males.[1] Such males tend to be unusually tall with long limbs; to be developmentally delayed and show testicular atrophy and sterility; and to have female-like breasts (gynecomastia) and body hair distribution. Klinefelter individuals also reportedly[2] can have various personality and behavioral challenges: Klinefelter syndrome may increase the risk of: Anxiety and depression. Social, emotional and behavioral problems, such as low self-esteem, emotional immaturity and impulsiveness. Infertility and problems with sexual function. In females, such individuals have three X chromosomes, or XXX instead of the normal XX. This is called triplo-X syndrome and occurs in every 900 to 1,000 live births.[3] That source says that XXX doesn’t usually cause any abnormalities in female appearance or function; at a cellular level, a cytologist can see that each cell inactivates two of the three X chromosomes; these show in cells as condensed Barr bodies and only one of the X chromosomes remains active. Barr bodies (inactivated X chromosomes) of a triplo-X female and a normal XX female.[4] If source 3 is correct, it would seem to me that we couldn’t accurately call the triplo-X condition a disease, as there are no symptoms and it would go unnoticed in the vast majority of such individuals. Only persons with some reason to get genetic testing would ever know they had it—just like some people can have two spleens or three kidneys and never know it unless it’s revealed as an incidental finding of a CT scan, surgery, or something like that. But source 3 may be wrong. A UK source[5] says of XXX females: Low self-esteem seems to be the most common feature, and shyness is also common in triple -X females. Receptive and expressive language disorders are common. These language disorders may be responsible for social problems, as is challenging behaviour, although this behaviour is less common. The frequency data I’ve given are from the U.S.-based National Organization for Rare Diseases (NORD) (references 1–2) and are flawed in two ways. One is that they say “males” for XXY but “live births” for XXX—two different standards of comparison. Does “males” mean only live-born males or include the stillborn? For the female data, does “live births” mean all live births or only live-born females? Is it 1 in 1,000 females or 1 in 1,000 people? For coming from a single source, this is carelessly inconsistent reporting and we can’t make a direct comparison. The other shortcoming of the NORD data is that they don’t say whether they mean the prevalence of these conditions globally or US only. It’s entirely possible that the data could vary between different countries. Both conditions result from abnormalities in meiosis called nondisjunction of the sex chromosomes—failure of a person’s sex chromosomes to separate normally in anaphase and go to different sperm or egg cells so each sex cell gets only one[6]—see my chart at the end of this essay. Nondisjunction occurs because of the failure of any one of three enzymes that normally causes chromosomes and chromatids to separate at anaphase,[7][8] and/or failure of a spindle assembly checkpoint (SAC)[9] that normally prepares mitotic and meiotic chromosomes for separation. I suspect few readers want to know any more detail about the enzymes or the SAC than that, so I won’t go into further depth here. They do raise a possibility in my mind, however, that the prevalence of XXY and XXX syndromes could vary geographically. One reason is that varying levels of environmental contaminants might (I’m only speculating) subject persons to mutations in the genes for those enzymes or SAC proteins, as might differences in diet, nutritional status, and food quality. For environmental reasons, the incidence of nondisjunction could hypothetically be different in a large urban population of Mumbai, Accra, or Shanghai than it is in Oslo, Helsinki, or Stockholm. Another is that these nondisjunction syndromes rise with the age of the mother, and countries differ significantly in life expectancy and ages at which females give birth. A country with older new mothers, on average, might be expected to have higher incidences of these and other nondisjunction disorders (such as Down syndrome). In the Hong Kong, the average mother has her first child at 32.8 years old; in Bangladesh, 25.7.[10] There might be even greater differences in the ages at which women have their last child. How much influence does this have on the incidence of congenital genetic disorders, including (speculatively) XXX and XXY? Some nondisjunction data, especially in older literature, suffers bias from the way the studies are done. There is seldom any reason to test newborns for these syndromes, so we really don’t know how common these syndromes are. Early studies often got their data from institutionalized individuals, as in psychiatric hospitals and prisons. If the reasons for institutionalization were in any way shaped by the presence of XXX or XXY chromosome sets, the data would not represent the population at large. Suppose, for example, the personality issues described in the two quotes above—low self-esteem, impulsive behaviors—influenced social isolation and behavioral problems that led to psychiatric or criminal institutionalization. In short, we should be suspicious of any such data unless the researchers have specified what measures they took to avoid sampling bias. Therefore, when any information source like NORD reports such data, they should ideally specify whether they mean global data or data for the U.S. or some other country only, and they (or more likely their primary sources) should describe the study population and show avoidance of sampling bias. All too many sources, though, are vague on these and other issues affecting the reported prevalence of various disorders. My search for better data from sources other than NORD hasn’t borne fruit so far, so this is about the best I can do for now to directly answer the QPG question. But it’s been, for me, an interesting exploration and thought exercise to start my day. Now I can log off, make some fresh coffee, and have breakfast. Question: Was President Obama ever known to have read the US Constitution?
Answer: Barack Obama was a professor of constitutional law at the University of Chicago from 1992 to 2004. Yes, he probably read the U.S. Constituion thoroughly and frequently. Not merely that (that’s the least of it!), but also hundreds of Supreme Court cases that have shaped constitutional law since 1803 (Marbury v. Madison)—just as I had to do when taking a constitutional law course and my professor knew the case law down pat. You can’t teach constitutional law anywhere (much less the U of Chicago) without a thorough knowledge of this case law. A lot of people have tried to cast doubt on Obama’s law professor credential. This is how the University of Chicago answered them (2nd emphasis added):[1] UC Law School statement: The Law School has received many media requests about Barack Obama, especially about his status as "Senior Lecturer." From 1992 until his election to the U.S. Senate in 2004, Barack Obama served as a professor in the Law School. He was a Lecturer from 1992 to 1996. He was a Senior Lecturer from 1996 to 2004, during which time he taught three courses per year. Senior Lecturers are considered to be members of the Law School faculty and are regarded as professors, although not full-time or tenure-track. The title of Senior Lecturer is distinct from the title of Lecturer, which signifies adjunct status. Like Obama, each of the Law School’s Senior Lecturers have high-demand careers in politics or public service, which prevent full-time teaching. Several times during his 12 years as a professor in the Law School, Obama was invited to join the faculty in a full-time tenure-track position, but he declined.

Question: What is the difference between endothelial cells and fibroblast cells?
Answer: Endothelial cells make up the inner lining of the heart, blood vessels, and lymphatic vessels. They’re a kind of epithelium called the simple squamous type, meaning a single layer of thin, flat cells. They have a bulge where the nucleus is, typically near the cell center. I often compare their shape to fried eggs, sunny side up, crowded together in a pan (the egg yolk resembles the shape of the cell nucleus and the egg white resembles the spread-out cell cytoplasm). Like eggs in a pan, endothelial cells touch each other along their edges, but more than touch, they’re physically attached to each other by intercellular junctions made of fibrous proteins, somewhat like a zipper holding together the two front panels of a jacket. This gives strength to the lining and regulates what chemicals can and cannot pass through the vessel wall, to or from the bloodstream. Below, the upper right figure is a view looking down on such cells from above, like looking down into the frying pan. The lower figure is looking at such cells forming a thin surface layer of an organ such as the stomach or intestine. (These are not endothelium, but endothelial cells have the same squamous shape and unilayered arrangement as these specimens.) Below is a section through the wall of an artery. The endothelium is only the barely visible, very thin surface layer. The bumps left and right of the arrowhead and elsewhere are the endothelial cell nuclei. (Blood flows through the space where the word endothelium is printed.) The rest of the tissue here is mainly smooth muscle. =========================================== Fibroblasts are not epithelial cells (not surface tissues), but fiber-producing cells of the connective tissues, such as the dermis of the skin and enclosing capsules of the internal organs such as the liver, kidneys, and spleen. They’re not flat, but variable in shape, commonly spindle-shaped: thick and roughly round in the middle and tapered toward both ends. At the ends, they often have long filamentous extensions. These are the cells that make most of the body’s collagen, among other products. Tendons and ligaments are made mainly by fibroblasts. Here are three images of fibroblasts. On the left in a thin section of loose connective tissue with four fibroblasts, identifiable by their dark purple nuclei. You can see the pale violet cell cytoplasm tapering away toward each side of the nucleus in a couple of them. The background shows fibers of collagen (broad pink bands) and elastin (slender violet filaments). The middle and right figures are fibroblasts grown in lab culture dishes. In the middle figure, fluorescent stains are used to show the fibroblast cytoplasm in green (note there is a lot of fiber in the cytoplasm itself) and nuclei in blue. The right photo shows living fibroblasts, unstained; the orange color is the microscope illumination, not a tissue stain.

Name: Ken Saladin
Question: Why do scientists take so long to prove something simple?
Answer: We don’t prove anything. We just disprove alternative hypotheses, and go tentatively with the one most consistent with the evidence we have at the time. If there’s enough evidence, then we call it a theory. Even then, different scientists can favor different theories for the same thing, such as the origin of COVID-19. As for “something simple,” nature is rarely if ever as simple as popular articles, TV shows, and Internet forums make them seem. Even as simple as the discovery I made for my doctoral dissertation—photosensory responses and sensory pigment in a larval blood fluke—it took me nearly two years of trial and error, near-tearful frustrations, complexities of experimental design to control for potentially interfering variables, designing and building my own apparatus, inconsistent data, inability one month to confirm results I thought I trusted the previous month—before I hit upon a solution. Once I reached that point, it took me about 6 weeks to get all the data that actually made it into the dissertation, and solve the problem. My dissertation data represent 6 weeks of research. They don’t tell the story of the 2 years that went before. At one point, I had nearly given up and decided to drop out of grad school and become a high-school biology teacher. Ideas that seem simple—either in foresight as we contemplate whether and how to tackle a problem, or in hindsight as we summarize, distill, simplify, and report them in our publications—have many complicating issues that nonscientists don’t see. I contend that of the three big branches of natural science, physics is the simplest because it deals with very elemental entities and variables: atoms and subatomic particles, quanta of energy, etc. (It’s quite likely also the most expensive of the three sciences—not everyone has their own particle accelerator or radiotelescope.) Physics seems hardest to many students because it’s so mathematical and it deals in abstract entities we can’t actually see with the eye, but only infer their existence and properties from their effects. (Have you ever seen an electron?) Chemistry comes next in complexity, because it deals with more complex systems—molecules and reaction mechanisms and their energy transfers and fallible predictions about what we can make from them. Still very mathematical but difficult and daunting for many students. When undergraduates are required to get a year of science no matter what they’re majoring in, the vast majority run away from physics and chemistry and flock to biology. Yet biology is the most complex of the three, because so many variables and chance elements enter into the phenomena we see. Because of these, we can seldom if ever be as certain of our interpretations of data as we can in the other sciences. We can’t control things as precisely. So often, when we publish, about the best we can say is tantamount to “there’s at least a 99.5% chance that this conclusion is true.” This is where statistical tests of significance comes in. If the best you can say is “There’s an 85% chance this is true,” you probably can’t even get that work published or past a dissertation committee because this isn’t a high enough level of confidence to think that anything real has been discovered. Pharmaceutical and medical sciences require the highest confidence levels of all because of the potential for human harm if we’re wrong. Companies can’t get a product to market unless there’s an extraordinarily low statistical uncertainty about its effectiveness and safety. One might say (with some exceptions) that biology is the least conclusive of the three big sciences. That’s because biologists study higher-order levels of complexity, ranging from macromolecules, organelles, and cells up to entire populations, ecosystems, and deep time. The more complex one’s object of study is, the more components there are in its structure (in morphological problems); the more links there are in the chain of causation (in physiological problems); the more variables enter into the observed effects, including variables we haven’t yet discovered or controlled for (even variables we can’t control, like effects of geomagnetic fields and ocean currents); and the more the outcome is simply subject to chance events. One of my favorite fields of biology is animal behavior, where there are so many fascinating stories to tell. When I read a report of an animal behavior in the journals or textbooks, or I see Sir David Attenborough present it so beautifully on film; or I’d tell my class of a certain behavioral study in 10 minutes of. lecture time—I must realize (and often told my students) that the “simple” and elegant little fact I just encountered or presented required over 20 years of field study not by just one researcher, but a whole team of professors and graduate students who sometimes had to camp out in tents in remote locations and bad weather for months at a time, year after year, to get that story. That’s what it takes, sometimes, to discover something “so simple.”

Name: Ken Saladin
Question: Can you provide an example of a non-cellular organism?
Answer: There’s no such thing, unless you consider viruses to be organisms. I don’t and I don’t think many biologists do, either. The very definition of life—or to be more precise, living things—practically starts with the premise that living things are composed of cells and cell products. At least on Earth, no one has ever found such a thing, or has any reason to think such a thing exists, as a living organism not composed of at least one cell. There’s no telling how we’d have to reconceptualize matters if we ever found lifelike entities on another planet, though. I would love to be around when that happened and the news broke. It would be one of the greatest revolutions in the history of science.

Question: We all know what a biologist does for a living, but what do evolutionists and evolution biologists do as a profession?
Answer: They do biology and paleontology as their professions. They do research on the phylogenetic history of living organisms and the evidence and mechanisms of evolution. There’s no difference in principle between one person being a biologist and geneticist, and another being a biologist and evolutionist. The second word in each case simply specifies what specialty they pursue within the scope of a biologist. Usually, in my experiences and among my colleagues, they won’t call themselves evolutionists, but that doesn’t mean it’s a term of creationist origin. Evolutionary scientists have used that term for themselves ever since Darwin. The evolutionary biologists in my department call themselves by more specific and informative terms such as paleobotanist and paleoherpetologist.

Question: How do humans defend against parasites? Is modern medicine the only way to get rid of them?
Answer: Most of the parasites I get, I get rid of by hand—ticks that I pick up doing yard work. But if you get internal parasites like amoebae or worms, then yes, modern medicine is the way to go. Folk remedies and what people misname “natural” cures aren’t very effective, if at all. Modern medicine is one of the two or three most important reasons we live significantly longer now than we did a century ago, and people in affluent countries today live longer than people in poorer ones. People who shun it are their own worst enemies.

Name: Ken Saladin
Question: Could amoebas possibly travel through my eye into the nasal cavity? Is this even a valid question? I brushed my inner eye corner after washing my hands with sink water and my paranoid mind is trying to cause worry. Doctor answers are appreciated.
Answer: It’s a valid question. There is a direct connection from the medial corner of each eye to the nasal cavity, called the nasolacrimal duct. It’s the reason why a person can fill the nasal cavity with anything from smoke to milk and squirt it out the corner of his eye (see YouTube), and why our nose runs when our eyes water. So it’s entirely conceivable for a pathogen to get from the eye to the nasal cavity. I have not heard of any definite cases of this, though. There is a serious bacterial pathogen, Chlamydia trachomatis, found in eye and nasal secretions and spread from person to person by contact with these secretions (often by face flies carrying them from person to person); it causes many cases of blindness in the tropics. I do not know and have not read of it traveling from eye to nose or vice versa, but there is some literature on it causing nasolacrimal duct obstruction, so eye-to-nose spread, or vicev versa, seems very plausible. But you asked about amoebae, not bacteria. If you’re thinking of the “brain-eating” amoeba Naegleria, I’m quite sure the answer to your question is no. There have really been few cases of this amoebic infection in history if we compare to other parasitic infections—only 133 cases as of 2014 —and none known to have invaded via the eye so far as I’ve ever read. There is, however, another free-living amoeba, Acanthamoeba, that can cause serious eye infections. It’s found in soil and water. People become infected through cuts and other wounds exposed to soil, inhalation of cysts in dust, and improper cleaning of contact lenses. Acanthamoeba has been found in lakes, swimming pools, tap water, and heating and air conditioning units. It’s known for causing severe eye infections (Acanthamoeba keratitis), which can cause permanent blindness. About 85% of cases have occurred in contact lens wearers. I’ve written more about it here:

Name: Ken Saladin
Question: Which herbivores display intraspecific aggression and kill each other? Why do they do this?
Answer: Yesterday I saw a video of a stallion viciously biting, carrying, and tossing a foal about, attempting to kill it, while the mare tried ineffectually to intercede. Why? I don’t know, but based on the behavior I do know of in other animals, I can make a reasonable guess. The foal was probably sired by a different stallion, a competitor. If this stallion kills it, he will not only eliminate some genes competing with his own for a place in the gene pool, but chances are, the mare will go into estrus (heat) sooner and may mate with him and propagate his genes. We see this sort of infanticide, for the same reason, in many animals. Sarah Blaffer Hrdy’s study of infanticide in Hanuman langurs (monkeys in India) is a classic on this subject. See “The Langurs of Abu” section in Sarah Blaffer Hrdy - Wikipedia. For a still broader perspective on animal infanticide, see Infanticide (zoology) - Wikipedia.

Name: Ken Saladin
Question: Why is elastin considered a fibre when it isn’t a bundle of subunits, instead just 1 long protein?
Answer: There’s nothing in the meaning of the word fiber (fibre) that requires that it be composed of “a bundle of subunits.” Nowhere in the biological, chemical, physical, or colloquial definition of fiber do I see any such stipulation. A fiber can be a cotton fiber, a length of sewing thread, an optical fiber, a carbon fiber, a length of spider silk, a nerve fiber, a muscle fiber, an elastic fiber, a collagen fiber, a cellulose fiber, a rayon or nylon fiber, or more. A fiber is simply any slender elongated material. As Wikipedia puts it, “Fiber or fibre is a natural or artificial substance that is significantly longer than it is wide.” That’s all.

Name: Ken Saladin
Question: Are the appendix and the coccyx proofs of evolution?
Answer: A good scientist avoids claiming that we have proved anything. There is no absolute proof, but degrees of probability that the evidence supports a given hypothesis or theory. The scientific mind must always be open to new evidence that may require modification or even abandonment of a previous conclusion. In evolution, there are so many lines of evidence consistent with the theory of natural selection—including the comparative anatomy of the mammalian appendix and coccyx—that we accept their evolutionary origin beyond reasonable doubt. The evidence of evolution is, in my opinion, stronger and more conclusive than the evidence often accepted in courts of law as “guilty beyond a reasonable doubt,” and that courts may use even to condemn a prisoner to death. Yet just as some prisoners are set free by new evidence that disproves their prior conviction (DNA, for example), so must we be willing to discard some evolutionary conclusions if disproven by new evidence. Contradictory as it might seem to laypeople, we can disprove scientific conclusions, but we can never prove them.

Question: Why doesn't our body use all of its glucagon stores for energy instead of converting muscle tissue protein into glucose?
Answer: You’re confusing glucagon (a pancreatic hormone) with glycogen (the energy-storage carbohydrate in muscle). We don’t use glucagon for energy; we use it to elevate blood glucose level (mainly by releasing glucose from the liver) in times of need, such as overnight and other long periods between meals. Glycogen is loosely called “animal starch” because it serves the same energy-storage function in animal cells that starch serves in plant cells. More importantly to your question, it’s undesirable to burn muscle protein for fuel, resulting in atrophy and loss of muscle mass and strength. That’s what happens in famine, eating disorders like anorexia, uncontrolled type 1 diabetes, the wasting away called cachexia in some cancers, and other muscle-wasting diseases. Cachexia. Muscle tissue has been burned as fuel to keep the body alive. One glycogen molecule can be made of 30,000 to 50,000 glucoses. If our cells hypothetically contained 30,000 or more glucose molecules for every 1 glycogen they actually do have, all that glucose would cause the cells to swell up with water (by osmosis) and either rupture or at least become very dysfunctional. Even as it is, 1 gram if glycogen absorbs and retains 3 grams of water. Storing so much glucose instead of glycogen would, at the very least, severely weaken one’s muscles and heart by overhydration. In very simple representation, here’s the difference between glycogen and glucose. Every one of the little green units is one glucose, and there are typically up to 30,000 of those per glycogen. Glycogen is a branching chain of glucoses strung together, curving curving around a core protein to form a compact glycogen granule in the cell. This drawing depicts a single glycogen granule with branching chains of glucose arranged around a central protein complex. There’s a lot of chemical energy (fuel) packed into each cytoplasmic granule like this. Even this depicts only a fraction of the 30,000 glucose units that may exist in one such complex. This is liver tissue stained to make the glycogen red, showing what an abundance of it we have in our livers, especially within the first few hours after a meal. Individual liver cells can be distinguished by their small violet nuclei. Here’s an electron micrograph of a small portion of a single liver cell in which the glycogen granules are stained black. Name: Ken Saladin
Question: What are the pros and cons of taking a 15 minute nap after lunch?
Answer: There are a lot of myths about negative effects of postprandial (after-meal) naps and siestas, but I don’t put any stock in them. I haven’t explored the subject deeply at a medical-physiological level, but I see no harm in it, and possible good. After a meal, our sympathetic “up-and-at-’em” nervous system is dialed down and the parasympathetic “resting and digesting” system is dialed up. The latter is the system that activates mechanisms in the stomach, intestines, and digestive glands for processing food. The sympathetic system, in contrast, inhibits digestion and redirects blood flow away from the GI tract to the muscles and other places where it may be more needed for physical activity. I say it seems a good idea to take a nap, turn down the sympathetic and turn up the parasympathetic, and let the latter do its job without interference. I’m with Gary Stark. I’m 75 now, and a 20-minute afternoon nap does wonders for me. I feel energized enough to go like the Energizer Bunny for hours after that. My motto: Kick back in the recliner and yield to your postprandial torpor.

Question: If Antibodies themselves typically do not pass directly through the cell membrane to enter the interior of the cell then how in the Antinuclear antibody (ANA) testing the antibodies bind to the nuclear proteins?
Answer: That’s a very intriguing question and sent me searching for answers. Web sites on ANA testing were no help, as they didn’t explain how the culprit autoantibodies get into the target cells in the first place. The first clue I picked up was this: Many or most cells have tiny dimples in the surface membrane called caveolae (“little caves”), 50–100 nm dia.[1] These are the most prominent surface feature of some cells, such as fat cells (adipocytes) and the walls of blood capillaries (endothelial cells). The cell membrane in the area of a caveola encloses droplets of the surrounding extracellular fluid (blood plasma in the case of endothelial cells), concentrating them in the pit. The pit becomes a flask-shaped vesicle that pinches off into the cytopasm of the cell. This one of the modes of cellular endocytosis. Caveolae of an adipocyte surface and diagram of their molecular relationship to the plasma membrane and extracellular molecules being taken up.[2] Inside the cell, the vesicle in many cases is opened by intracellular enzymes and releases its cargo into the cytoplasm. This is how cells take up blood proteins such as albumin and insulin and how some blood components can cross the capillary wall, without opening the vesicles, to get into the surrounding tissue fluid. The combination of events from uptake on one side of a cell to release of molecules like insulin on the other side is called transcytosis, pictured below. Some pathogenic bacteria and viruses—far larger than antibodies of course—also enter their target cells this way. HIV, SARS-CoV-2 (the COVID virus), and some pathogenic strains of E. coli are examples of this. (Figure from my own book, Anatomy & Physiology—The Unity of Form and Function, 10th ed., (McGraw Hill, 2024) Caveolae are the mechanism by which antinuclear antibodies (ANAs) enter target cells,[3] setting the stage for many autoimmune diseases—attacks of a misguided immune system against one’s own tissues.[4][5] ANAs in the blood plasma can be detected by clinical laboratory tests and afford one of the tools for diagnosing autoimmune diseases.[6] Up to 30% of us have detectable ANAs in the blood[7]; what triggers autoimmune disease in only a fraction of these, I don’t know (does anyone?). The next question is how do ANAs enter the target cell nucleus? The nucleus is enclosed in a membrane of its own, perforated with holes called nuclear pores. Not merely holes, though, each pore is encircled in a multiprotein complex that acts as a selective gate, regulating what can enter or leave the nucleus (such as nucleotides, amino acids, steroid hormones, and other signaliing molecules getting in and mRNA molecules getting out). For some pretty cool electron micrographs showing these pores in greater magnification and near-molecular detail, see my earlier Quora discussion.[8] Electron micrograph of the nuclear surface showing its numerous pores, and diagram of the molecular organization of a pore. (EM photo from my own textbook cited previously; drawing from The Scientist magazine.[9]) These pores are ~5.2 nm wide in humans. Antibodies in the IgG class measure ~14.5 x 8.5 x 4.0 nm,[10] so it looks in theory like it could fit through a nuclear pore. Most ANAs are in the IgG class, but some are larger IgA and IgM antibodies that, it might seem, would be excluded from the nucleus by molecular size alone (especially IgM, more than five times the size of IgG). (Reference for the antibody classes of ANAs is Medscape,[11] but requires registration to view it.) Migration through a nuclear pore is more complex than a simple matter of molecule size v. pore size, though; it depends on recognition and “acceptance” by the gate-regulating proteins of the nuclear pore complex. Possibly these autoantibodies “trick” the gate proteins in some manner analogous to the way HIV and SARS-CoV-2 (the COVID virus) trick their target cells into taking up the viruses. We must also bear in mind that even the subunits of a ribosome, made in the nucleus, can and must get out through these pores to perform their protein-synthesizing role in the cytoplasm. These are enormous (25–30 nm) compared to the size of a nuclear pore. No doubt their mode of transenvelope transport has long been heavily researched and understood, but I won’t go down that heavily traveled road “through the yellow wood” just now. As of 2018, “a deep understanding of the penetration mechanisms of autoantibody and the extent to which they may be modified is still lacking”.[12] It seems a safe bet that scientists are vigorously working on this problem, given the importance to so many devastating autoimmune diseases that assail us. Your question pointed me down an interesting path of exploration and discovery. Thanks. I hope this helps answer your question at least as far as I was able to get with it.

Question: Why did the wings of bats evolve to be weaker than that of birds?
Answer: Bats and birds both started out from different wingless ancestors and separately evolved wings adapted to their respective advantages. Bats evolved stronger wings and pectoral muscles than some small birds—sparrows, juncos, and chickadees, for example—whereas some birds evolved the strongest wings and pectoral muscles of all, such as raptors, vultures, seabirds, and long-distance migrators. Yet the fact that a migrating monarch butterfly can travel 4,000 to 4,800 km (2,500 to 3,000) miles shows us that strong wings aren’t always necessary for long-distance flight. A fairly common U.S. species, the Mexican free-tailed bat, often flies 100 miles each night just to hunt down enough to eat, and flies from Texas and Arizona to as far as Central America to spend each winter. But there is a European bat, Nathusius’s pipstrelle, that flies at least 2,486 km (> 1,500 mi) from northwestern Russia to the Alps of southern France in 63 days.[1] And that’s a straight-line distance; their actual flight path is probably longer. Such examples don’t suggest weak wings to me. The insect-eating bats have to be adapted for maneuverability to catch enough flying insects to sustain themselves, rather than for higher-powered straight flight. More bat species pass the northern winters in hibernation than escape the cold by migration, such as the most common one in my area, the little brown bat. Northern bats overwinter locally in caves, mines, rock crevices, hollow trees, buildings, etc. So given that their need for maneuvering outweighs any need for long-distance flight, it’s not surprising that they have a more fluttering flight and smaller wings and pectoral muscles than many birds. One colony of Mexican free-tailed bats can consume 250 tons of moths and other insects in one night! It’s a spectacular sight to see them fly out each night under the Congress Street bridge in Austin, Texas and go flying down the Colorado River in search of their nightly tonnage of insects. One can get a similar show at the Carlsbad Caverns in New Mexico, but less impressive to me than the Austin emergence. There are 1.5 million bats living under Austin’s bridge alone. They look like a meandering plume of smoke as they recede into the distance downriver. If you’re going to stand under the bridge to watch their evening emergence, you’d better take an umbrella. They lighten their load, so to speak, as they embark on their flight. It does not make good hair conditioner. Local folks say you can always tell the tourists—they walk under the bridge and look up, risking a facefull of bat excreta. The locals stay out of the bridge. Question: How long does protein synthesis take?
Answer: Assuming you mean protein synthesis in a living cell, not in a laboratory, it’s not long at all. It’s so fast it’s hard even to believe it. Plasma cells—the body’s antibody-producing cells (antibodies are proteins)—produce about 2,000 molecules per second (per cell), an average of 0.5 millisecond for each protein molecule. I can’t even say “protein” 2,000 times a second. However, that’s the figure for total cell output, with thousands of ribosomes in each plasma cell working simultaneously to make copies of the same protein. At the level of a single ribosome, it reportedly takes from 20 seconds to several minutes to make one protein molecule. Any cell’s total protein output is at a much greater rate though, because it has thousands of mRNA molecules coding for the same protein being translated at once, and each mRNA being simultaneously translated by typically 10 to 20 ribosomes at once. Question: Why is an enzyme considered a protein?

It can mean 10 or 10,000. Almost all enzymes—all those one usually hears about, unless one is a biochemist, geneticist, or biologist—are polypeptides. Some RNA molecules are also considered enzymes (ribozymes) because of their catalytic function. If we disregard the ribozymes for present purposes, we can define enzyme as any protein that serves a catalytic function. That is, enzymes are a subset of proteins.

Question: What are the advantages of mammals?
Answer: Most mammal species are nocturnal,[1][2] a fact that most people aren’t aware of (and may doubt) because our own species is diurnal and we just don’t notice the nocturnal ones as much. Nocturnal behavior in early mammals, made possible by their warm and stable body temperatures, gave them an advantage over the dinosaurs and other reptiles with which they coexisted. Carnivorous reptiles hunted by day because they needed to warm up in the sun to be fast and agile enough to hunt successfully. Being nocturnal also kept the mammals relatively hidden from danger by day.[3] Further, it enabled them to turn the tables on the predatory dinosaurs; some mammals raided dinosaur nests and ate the eggs and probably the hatchlings, a brazen move easier to do at night. Ability to spread to colder climates, and pregnancy (carrying the fetuses internally instead of having to defend a nest site), were likely also important to mammalian success.

Question: What are the disadvantages of mammals?
Answer: With a metabolic rate higher than that of fish, amphibians, and reptiles, mammals require more food, they must spend a larger portion of their time searching for and consuming it, and they are less tolerant of food-poor habitats and periods of food scarcity. Among other consequences, this is why reptiles were successful in colonizing the Galapagos Islands (and other oceanic islands) by drifting from nearby continents on floating mats of vegetation, but very few mammals were able to do so. Mammals usually could not survive the long periods of starvation at sea. Another factor is probably that mammals could not minimize evaporative water loss from the skin and sweat glands as well as reptiles (with scales and no sweat glands) can. Also, to support their higher metabolism, mammals generally require faster respiratory rates, and lose a lot of water in every exhaled breath. In humans, each expired breath is about 12% water, and we lose about 300 mL of water per day through breathing (at average atmospheric humidity).

Question: What is the reason for humans not having an enzyme to break down theobromine?
Answer: Humans DO have the enzymes to break it down; it’s dogs and cats that don’t. The reason humans do and other mammals do not metabolize it is presumably the evolution of chocolate consumption and, hence, tolerance of this toxin. As in milk consumption and the evolution of human lactose tolerance (aka lactase persistence—note the spelling difference), metabolic enzymes can evolve in a matter of mere thousands of years when there is an adaptive advantage to being able to use certain foods that are available. The consumption of chocolate began about 5,300 years ago among the Mayo-Chinchipe culture (in what is now southeastern Ecuador), and spread thorugh Mesoamerica to the Olmec people of what is now southern Mexico. The Olmecs were consuming chocolate by about 1900 BCE (~3900 years ago). It was consumed as a bitter drink thought to improve male virility and fertility. Compounds related to theobromine are found as well in some other nutritionally useful plants. It’s not surprising at all that humans evolved increasing tolerance of plant toxins as they benefitted from a broader range of usable foods. Compare lactase persistence—the ability to digest milk sugar, lactose, and thus consume milk products without adverse effects. DNA analysis of ancient European skeletons shows that an MCM6 gene mutation enabling lactose digestion arose about 4,300 years ago. (Lactase persistence has evolved independently in other areas as well, including Subsaharan Africa and Mongolia.) If a gene enabling humans to digest lactose can become established in 4,300 years, then there’s no surprise in seeing a gene enabling tolerance of theobromine becoming established in 5,300 years in Mesoamerica. There is no reason for dogs, as carnivores, ever to have consumed or benefited from cacao, and thus no reason for them to evolve the means to detoxify theobromine. Theobromine, caffeine, and other such alkaloids are among the poisons plants produce to protect themselves from insects and herbivorous vertebrates.

Question: What is coelomic fluid?
Answer: Most animals have an internal body cavity called the coelom (pronounced SEE-loam)—ours consists of the thoracic and abdominal cavities and is divided by the diaphragm. The watery solution in that cavity that bathes our internal organs is called the coelomic fluid. Depending on its location and the partitions between locations, it also has other more specific names. I think our own peritoneal fluid, pericardial fluid, and pleural fluid are all considered coelomic fluids, whereas other internal body fluids are not: blood, lymph, synovial fluid of the joints, cerebrospinal fluid of the central nervous system, aqueous humor of the eye, etc. Among invertebrates with open circulatory systems (such as insects), the coelomic fluid is called hemolymph. Among invertebrate animals, coelomic fluid is pressurized and provides physical support for the body called a hydrostatic skeleton. Acted upon by the animal’s muscles, it enables movements in animals ranging from nematodes and earthworms to insects and crustaceans. Circular constriction of an earthworm’s muscles, for example, pushes the head end of the worm forward, and then contraction of the longitudinal body-wall muscles pulls the tail forward. In insects and spiders, coelomic fluid pressure extends the legs whereas muscles flex them. This why dead insects and spiders commonly have the legs flexed—coelomic fluid (hemolymph) pressure is lost when the heart stops beating.

Question: What are enzymes? Do they only work in living organisms?
Answer: An enzyme is an organic molecule that acts as a catalyst in the body’s metabolic reactions. Some of them are made of RNA (ribozymes),[1] but most of them are proteins.[2] Most of them function inside human cells, but some function externally, especially the digestive enzymes of the saliva, stomach, pancreas, and small intestine. Beyond the scope of humans, enzymes also function externally in the way houseflies digest food and mushrooms and other fungi digest wood and other dead plant matter, both by secreting enzymes onto them. These organisms then suck up or absorb the nutrients released by external enzymatic digestion. Enzymes are now common in commercial products including laundry detergents, dishwasher detergents, and other cleaning agents. Innumerable biology students, including hundreds of my own, have performed simple lab experiments digesting starch and proteins in test tubes with the aid of enzymes. Many enzymes can be purchased from biological and chemical supply companies in powdered form for teaching, research, and industrial uses. Enzymes have numerous commercial uses far beyond their roles in living organisms, including manufacturing and the food industry.[3] [4] Numerous chemists are employed in the area of industrial enzymology.

Some cell types, including muscle, have many times as much ATP as they would need if its only purpose was to provide energy for contraction or other functions.

Question: What is the relation between catecholamines and ATP, CNS stimulants and ATP?

CNS stimulants are diverse and don’t fit into any one category. Amphetamine, perhaps the most widely known CNS stimulant (if you asked random people to name one), shares some features with catecholamines, but not the catechol or –OH groups. Caffeine, the most popular stimulant, has a little bit in common with ATP and adenosine, but not with catecholamines—no benzene rings, no hydroxyl or amino groups. Cocaine, compared to these others, is sui generis—in a class by itself.

Question: What are the potential issues with using adult stem cells compared to embryonic stem cells in medical treatment? Are there any advantages to using one type over the other?
Answer: In effect, skin grafts are a type of stem-cell treatment. It’s the adult stem cells in the grafted skin (from somewhere else on the same person’s body if possible) that multiply to fill the space formerly occupied by the lost skin. A limitation of adult stem cells (ASCs) is that they can’t multiply and produce just any cell type that might be desirable. Most ASCs are limited to one or a few types of cells they can develop into. Embryonic stem cells are much less limited—described as pluripotent because they can develop into a broad range (pluri-, “many) of mature cell types. I don’t think embryonic stem cells are used very much anymore because of limited availability and controversy. It’s now possible to “reprogram” ASCs into “induced pluripotent stem cells” (iPSCs) with a greater range of developmental potential—such as (in theory) reprogramming bone marrow or fat cells into iPSCs that can replace muscle, spinal cord, or pancreatic cells. Not much of this has yet reached clinical practice though—the technical difficulties and uncertainties still stand as obstacles. For example, we don’t know if stem cells could develop into a tumor instead of the intended tissue.

Question: How are marine mammals able to sleep underwater?
Answer: Dolphins, for one, sleep at the water surface, breathing normally.[1] Some larger whales also lie either motionless, or swim slowly, at the surface with their blowholes in the air. Sperm whales, however, sleep near the surface in a head-up position and swim to the surface for a breath of air every several minutes. Whales can hold their breaths for as long as 45 minuts to 2 hours[2]—plenty of time for a long nap. Sea otters sleep at the surface lying on their backs with their noses above water. In kelp forests, they commonly wrap a bit of kelp around themselves to stay in place and not drift out into less protected waters where hungry sharks and orcas may roam.[3] Some even sleep holding hands with their neighbors to help each other to not drift away. Manatees and dugongs lie on their backs underwater to sleep, surfacing to breathe every 20 minutes or so.[4][5] Dugongs sleep only in short bursts.[6] Sea lions and seals sleep both on land and in the water.[7] Polar bears[8]sleep on land or on sea ice. I don’t think they ever sleep in the water (much less underwater, as the question puts it). With their body fat and waterproof fur, polar bears are very buoyant and it would require a lot of energy to stay underwater—not conducive to sleeping. Besides that, the water is extremely deep in their habitat. I don’t think they ever sleep floating with their noses out of water. Walruses sleep both on land and (for shorter periods) in the water. In the water, they sleep either lying on their backs at the surface, ot vertically, bobbing up and down with their heads above water. They can also sleep lying on the bottom.[9] A surprising thing about dolphins, other whales, seals, dugongs, and manatees is that only half of the brain sleeps at one time, the other half remaining awake and alert.[10] This is called unihemispheric sleep. We and most other mammals can’t do that; both cerebral hemispheres sleep at the same time.

Question: Why is it much easier to lift your leg above 90 degrees when the knee is bent? My elbow has no impact on arm rotation at the shoulder. Is there some connection between the knee and hip joints that the elbow and shoulder lack?

On the back of the thigh are three hamstring muscles—the biceps femoris, semimembranosus, and semitendinosus (see lower left labels). These muscles attach at the upper end to the lower pelvic girdle (specifically to the ischial tuberosity of the pelvis). They cross the entire posterior thigh and attach at the lower end to the upper ends of the tibia and fibula of the leg, just below the knee. One of their actions is to flex the knee; another is to extend (straighten) the hip joint, as when you rise from a sitting or squatting position. Muscles of the gluetal and posterior thigh regions. The right side of the figure is a deeper dissection than the left. The hamstrings are superficial muscles shown on both sides, but the right side best shows their pelvic attachments. • Here’s my best guess at an answer to your question. When one is standing straight up, the hamstrings are stretched almost as far as possible. If you keep your knee straight and raise the entire lower limb, that stretches the hams even more, and when they’re stretched to the maximum, you can’t raise the limb any farther. But if you flex your knee, the hamstrings get shorter. Then when you raise your thigh, you stretch them. Since they were shortened by knee flexion, that allows thigh elevation to stretch them more. Hence, prior flexion of the knee enables one to raise the thigh higher than 90°.

Question: What is aging, really? We certainly see a lot of 'causes' and factors and processes, but do we really understand what it is? How can we modify this process?
Answer: Strictly speaking, aging is just growing older—the passage of time. The degeneration of organs and tissues that accompanies aging is better called senescence. There are multiple causes of senescence. Like anything else, cells, tissues, and organs wear out. The rate of mitosis slows down, old cells that die aren’t replaced as fast as when the body was younger, and we thus see various degenerative changes throughout the body: bones, muscles, ligaments, brain, nerves, eyes, ears, immune system, endocrine system, heart, blood vessels, lungs, kidneys, stomach—the whole show. Among the reasons for this are cumulative oxidative damage to molecules and cells (like the rusting of iron and the yellowing of old newspaper); progressive loss of telomeres from the chromosomes of dividing cells, placing a limit on how many times a cell line can divide; slowing rates of cell division and replacement; cumulative DNA damage (the DNA of an average human cell is damaged 100,000 times per day!); less effective DNA repair responses (which repair most of these damaging events in younger bodies, less so in older bodies); cross-linking of proteins (responsible for increasing stiffness in the joints, lenses of the eyes, and lessening resiliency of the skin); increasingly abnormal protein structures for reasons other than DNA mutations or damage; and increasing autoimmune diseases (the immune system attacking one’s own cells).

Question: When will vestigial organs be no longer in the biology of animals?

Question: Do nerve cells have a single nucleus with only one copy of DNA? If so, how do they divide during mitosis without doubling up on chromosomes first?

Question: In DNA, there are 23 pairs of chromosomes, which means 46 single chromosomes, and so 92 strands, am I right?
Answer: Between the S phase of the cell cycle and telophase of mitosis, a diploid cell has 92 molecules of DNA—46 chromosomes, two chromatids each, with one DNA in each chromatid. From telophase to the S phase, it has 46, with one chromatid and DNA each.
